title: Given the head of a linked list that contains a cycle, return the node where the cycle begins. If there is no cycle, return null. Solve it with constant extra space. (LeetCode: Linked List Cycle II)
shortTitle: Start of LinkedList Cycle (Finding the Loop Entry Node)

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the start of a linked list cycle extends Floyd's algorithm. First the tortoise and hare meet inside the loop, confirming a cycle. Then you reset one pointer to the head and advance both pointers one step at a time; the node where they meet again is the cycle's entry point. This works because of a distance relationship between the head, the loop start, and the meeting point, and it uses constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh confirmed that a chain of transaction records loops, and now he needs to find the exact record where the loop rejoins the chain, because that is the corrupted pointer he must fix. After the fast and slow readers meet inside the loop, he moves one reader back to the very start of the chain and then walks both readers forward at the same slow pace. The spot where they meet again is precisely the record where the loop begins.
s1_definition.oneliner: After the pointers meet in the loop, send one back to the head and walk both one step at a time; they meet at the loop's start.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the start of a linked list cycle extends Floyd's algorithm. First the tortoise and hare meet inside the loop, confirming a cycle. Then you reset one pointer to the head and advance both pointers one step at a time; the node where they meet again is the cycle's entry point. This works because of a distance relationship between the head, the loop start, and the meeting point, and it uses constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh confirmed that a chain of transaction records loops, and now he needs to find the exact record where the loop rejoins the chain, because that is the corrupted pointer he must fix. After the fast and slow readers meet inside the loop, he moves one reader back to the very start of the chain and then walks both readers forward at the same slow pace. The spot where they meet again is precisely the record where the loop begins.

**One line to remember:** After the pointers meet in the loop, send one back to the head and walk both one step at a time; they meet at the loop's start.

sections.s2_technical:
This builds on cycle detection. First we run the tortoise and hare: slow moves one, fast moves two, until they either meet, confirming a cycle, or fast runs off the end, meaning no cycle, in which case we return null.

Once they meet inside the loop, we use a distance property. Let the distance from the head to the loop start be some value, call it the entry distance. Let the distance from the loop start to the meeting point be another value. Because the fast pointer traveled exactly twice as far as the slow pointer when they met, algebra shows that the entry distance equals the loop length minus the distance from the loop start to the meeting point, which in turn equals the distance from the meeting point forward around the loop back to the start. The practical consequence is simple: if we reset one pointer to the head and keep the other at the meeting point, then advance both one node at a time, they will meet exactly at the loop start.

A finance usage example: suppose the chain is `T1 -> T2 -> T3 -> T4 -> T5 -> T3`, where T5 loops back to T3. The tortoise and hare meet somewhere inside the loop among T3, T4, T5. We then put one pointer back at T1 and leave the other at the meeting point, and advance both one step at a time. They meet at T3, which is exactly where the loop begins and the corrupted pointer originates.

The senior-level nuance: the correctness rests on the two-to-one speed relationship, which guarantees the fast pointer has covered twice the slow pointer's distance at the meeting moment, and the resulting equation is what makes resetting to the head land both pointers at the entry. A common mistake is advancing the reset pointer at double speed in the second phase; in the second phase both pointers must move at the same single-step speed. If the meeting never happens, there is no cycle and no entry node to return.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's integrity team has already detected that a transaction chain contains a loop, but detection alone is not enough; the repair tool must know the exact record where the loop rejoins the chain, because that record holds the corrupted next pointer that must be reset. Finding that entry record by storing every visited node is too memory-heavy for huge chains.

Problem 2 — The repair must run in constant extra space, so the team uses the extended Floyd algorithm that locates the loop entry using only pointers.

The code defines a `CycleEntryLocator` class with a `findCycleStart` method that first detects the meeting point and then resets one pointer to the head to find the entry node. A runnable demo builds a looping chain and logs the identifier of the loop's starting record.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the chain `T1 -> T2 -> T3 -> T4 -> T5 -> T3`, where T5 loops back to T3.

Step 1: In phase one, slow and fast both start at T1. Slow advances one and fast advances two each iteration. Slow visits T2, T3, T4, and fast visits T3, T5, then wraps into the loop. Eventually inside the loop, slow and fast land on the same node, confirming a cycle, and the loop breaks with slow at the meeting point.

Step 2: Phase two begins. A new pointer is placed at the head T1, while slow stays at the meeting point inside the loop.

Step 3: Both pointers now advance one node at a time. The head pointer walks T1, T2, toward T3, and the meeting-point pointer walks around the loop at the same pace.

Step 4: Because of the distance relationship, the two pointers meet exactly at T3. The head pointer arrives at T3 at the same moment the other pointer arrives at T3 coming around the loop.

Step 5: The method identifies T3 as the loop entry, logs a severe message naming the record, and returns the T3 node so the repair tool knows exactly which next pointer to reset.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 6:50:00 PM com.bank.repair.CycleEntryDemo main
SEVERE: Cycle starts at record T3
INFO: Loop entry record = T3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the node where a linked list cycle begins is a two-phase extension of Floyd's tortoise and hare algorithm, and it still runs in linear time with constant extra space. The first phase is ordinary cycle detection: a slow pointer moving one node at a time and a fast pointer moving two nodes at a time, which either meet inside the loop, confirming a cycle, or the fast pointer runs off the end, meaning there is no cycle and no entry node to return.

Once the two pointers meet inside the loop, the second phase uses a distance relationship. Because the fast pointer traveled exactly twice as far as the slow pointer when they met, a little algebra shows that the distance from the head to the loop start equals the distance from the meeting point onward around the loop back to the start. The practical upshot is elegant: I reset one pointer to the head, leave the other at the meeting point, and then advance both one node at a time at the same speed, and the node where they meet is exactly the start of the cycle.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a repair tool. The integrity checker had already told us a transaction chain contained a loop, but to fix it the repair tool needed the exact record where the loop rejoined the chain, because that record held the corrupted next pointer that had to be reset. The chains were huge and we ran under tight memory limits, so storing every visited record was not an option, and the extended Floyd algorithm located the loop entry using only pointers.

The senior-level point I emphasize is the one detail people get wrong: in the second phase both pointers must move at the same single-step speed, not at the original two-to-one ratio. The whole correctness argument depends on the two-to-one speed only during detection, which produces the distance equation; once I reset to the head, equal-speed stepping is what makes the two pointers converge on the entry. Being able to explain why the distances line up, rather than just reciting the steps, is what demonstrates I truly understand the algorithm.
